old: Classical Hungarian essayistic rhetoric relies heavily on periodic symmetry (*körmondat*). Correlative pairs like *egyfelől... másfelől* (on the one hand... on the other hand) or *nemcsak... hanem... is* (not only... but also) establish an intellectual cadence that demonstrates rigorous deliberation (*mérlegelés*) and fairness (*pártatlanság*).
new: You know *egyrészt … másrészt* from B1 Unit 4 and *nemcsak … hanem … is* from A2 Unit 5. In an essay, *egyfelől … másfelől* (on the one hand … on the other hand) does the same job as *egyrészt … másrészt*. Several balanced clauses together make a *körmondat* (periodic sentence), which weighs a question (*mérlegelés*) fairly and without bias (*pártatlanság*).

old: Advanced argumentation requires explicit signaling of logical transitions. In C1 writing, instead of simple *ezért* or *így*, sophisticated authors use compound relational expressions like *ennek fényében* (in light of this) to re-evaluate previous evidence, or *mindebből következően* (consequently from all this) to launch a deductive breakthrough.
new: You know *ezért*, *következésképpen* and *ennélfogva* from B1 Unit 32. In an essay, *ennek fényében* (in light of this) re-evaluates earlier evidence, and *mindebből következően* (consequently from all this) draws the conclusion from a whole chain of arguments.

old: When holding firm against accumulated counter-evidence or adversity, *mindezek dacára* (in spite of all this) conveys a resolute rhetorical defiance:
new: You know *dacára* and *ellenére* from B1 Unit 29. *Mindezek dacára* (in spite of all this) holds firm against everything said before:
